title: The Altar by the Jordan
summary: Joshua sends the eastern tribes (Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh) home across the Jordan with his blessing, their promise to fight alongside their brothers kept. On the way they build a large altar by the river, and the western tribes, fearing rebellion against the LORD, gather for war. A delegation led by Phinehas the priest confronts them, learns that the altar is a memorial and not a place of sacrifice, and returns satisfied, and civil war is averted.
story: The land has been conquered and divided (chapters 13 to 21), and the book has just declared that not one of God's good promises to Israel failed (21:45). One loose thread remains. Long before, in Numbers 32, the tribes of Reuben and Gad and half of Manasseh asked Moses for the grazing lands east of the Jordan, and Moses agreed on condition that their fighting men cross over and help the others take Canaan. They did, and now they go home. This chapter asks a question that will matter for the rest of Israel's history: can a people split by a river remain one people under one God? The near miss here also looks ahead to Judges, where the tribes will not always talk before they fight.
historical:
The setting is the end of Joshua's campaigns, with the tabernacle now standing at Shiloh in the hill country of Ephraim (18:1). The Jordan valley was a real divide. The river runs deep in a rift below sea level, and the lands east of it, Gilead and Bashan, lay in a different geography, closer to the Ammonites and Moabites and farther from the sanctuary. The worry voiced by the eastern tribes, that later generations would say the Jordan marked the edge of the LORD's people, was not far-fetched. The site called Geliloth (the word suggests a circle or ring of stones) has not been securely identified; it may be the same place as Gilgal, where Israel first camped after crossing, though that is uncertain.

The story leans on two remembered disasters. At Peor (Numbers 25), Israelite men joined in the worship of Baal of Peor with Moabite women, a plague broke out, and Phinehas stopped it by killing an Israelite man and a Midianite woman. And at Jericho, Achan took plunder devoted to the LORD, and Israel was defeated at Ai (Joshua 7). In both cases one group's sin brought judgment on the whole people. That is why the western tribes react so quickly.
cultural:
Deuteronomy 12 commanded Israel to bring its sacrifices only to the place the LORD would choose, not to set up altars wherever they liked. The single sanctuary was meant to keep Israel's worship from blending with the local shrines of Canaan, and it expressed that Israel was one people under one God. A second altar, especially a large and conspicuous one, looked like a rival sanctuary and so like a breach of the covenant.

In the ancient Near East, standing stones, cairns, and altars were common as memorials and boundary markers, recording an agreement or an event for later generations. The eastern tribes claim this is what they built: a replica (verse 28), a copy of the LORD's altar at Shiloh that was never meant for burnt offerings, standing as a witness that they too belonged to the LORD. The word for replica can mean a pattern or model, the same word used for the plan of the tabernacle in Exodus 25:9. The ten chiefs sent with Phinehas, one for each western tribe, show how seriously the matter was treated: this was a formal inquiry by the whole congregation.
literary: The chapter has two parts. Verses 1 to 8 close the story of the conquest with Joshua's farewell to the eastern tribes, a speech that sums up the covenant life in a string of verbs: love, walk, keep, hold fast, serve. Verses 9 to 34 form a tense dispute story built on accusation and answer. The accusing speech (verses 16 to 20) piles up the words for unfaithfulness and rebellion and reaches back to Peor and Achan. The reply opens with a solemn double oath (“The LORD, the Mighty One, is God! The LORD, the Mighty One, is God!”) and turns the accusation around: the altar is not a sign of leaving the LORD but of clinging to him. The key word throughout is witness, and the chapter ends where it began, with the naming of the altar. The Hebrew of verse 34 doesn't clearly give a name, and translations like the BSB supply Witness from the sense of the sentence.

outline.t: Joshua commends and blesses the eastern tribes
The altar at Geliloth and Israel's alarm
Phinehas and the chiefs accuse them of breaking faith
The eastern tribes explain: a witness, not a rival altar
The delegation is satisfied and war is averted

doctrines.note: Joshua's charge in verse 5 sums up what the covenant asks: love for God expressed in obedience, loyalty, and wholehearted service. Israel's unity is covenantal; the tribes belong together because they belong to the same God.
The western tribes' fear shows how seriously Israel took the danger of false worship after Peor. Worship on one's own terms, even of the true God, was treated as a first step toward leaving him.

The chapter models how God's people should handle suspected unfaithfulness: take it seriously, send trusted leaders, speak directly, listen to the answer, and rejoice when the fear proves unfounded. It also shows how quickly misunderstanding can divide a people who share the same faith.

words.note: Mizbeach, altar, from the verb for slaughtering a sacrifice. It appears twelve times in this chapter, and everything turns on what kind of altar this is. An altar for offerings would rival the one before the tabernacle; an altar that is only a copy, standing as a sign, is something else. Same word, two very different meanings.

Ma'al, unfaithfulness or breach of faith. It describes betrayal of trust, often of a sacred obligation, and is the word used for Achan's sin in Joshua 7:1. The western tribes use it to frame the altar as treachery against God.

Ed, witness. A witness in Hebrew can be a person or an object that testifies to an agreement, like the heap of stones Jacob and Laban set up in Genesis 31. The eastern tribes' answer rests on this word: the altar speaks to future generations about who they belong to.

Marad, to rebel. It describes revolt against a lawful authority, as of a vassal against an overlord. Its repetition in verses 16 to 19 and 29 shows how the western tribes read the altar: as a political and religious revolt against the LORD, Israel's true king.

christ: The dispute is about who has a share in the LORD, and whether a boundary can shut some of God's people out. The New Testament takes up the same question on a larger scale. Paul says that in Christ the dividing wall of hostility between Jew and Gentile has been torn down, so that both have access in one Spirit to the Father (Ephesians 2:14-18). The single altar at Shiloh pointed to one place of meeting with God; the letter to the Hebrews presents Christ's once-for-all sacrifice as the one offering by which God's people are made holy (Hebrews 10:10-14). The link here is thematic rather than predictive. The chapter's longing for unity in true worship finds its fulfillment in the one sacrifice and the one people formed around it.

hard.q: Weren't the western tribes wrong to rush toward war before they knew the facts?
hard.a: They did assemble for war first (verse 12), but they didn't march. They sent a delegation of priests and leaders to ask, and they accepted the answer. Some readers see the chapter as praising their zeal for God's honor, given what Peor and Achan had cost. Others see a warning about how quickly suspicion can turn to violence, and note that Judges 20 later tells of a civil war that did go ahead. Many readers hold the two together: the chapter commends zeal for God's honor, and it shows that the readiness to listen is what kept that zeal from ending in bloodshed.

questions: The eastern tribes feared their children would be told they had no share in the LORD. What kinds of boundaries today make some people feel shut out of God's people?
When have you, or a community you belong to, assumed the worst about someone before asking? What might Phinehas's delegation teach about how to respond?
Joshua's charge in verse 5 lists five things: love, walk, keep, hold fast, serve. Which of these is hardest for you, and why?
